---
title: "Preparing CHIRPS"
subtitle: "Monthly precipitation v3.0, from either the NetCDF or the GeoTIFF distribution"
---

## What CHIRPS is

CHIRPS is a quasi-global precipitation dataset from the Climate Hazards Center
at UC Santa Barbara, blending satellite estimates with station observations. It
runs from 1981 to the present at 0.05 degrees, and for SPI it is the usual
choice where rainfall is the only variable you need.

::: {.callout-important}
## CHIRPS is not global

The grid covers **60S to 60N**, not pole to pole. Measured from the v3.0 monthly
GeoTIFF: 2400 rows by 7200 columns, bounds `lat -60.0 .. 60.0`,
`lon -180.0 .. 180.0`.

Anything above 60N or below 60S is outside the product, not missing from it.
Plan your analysis domain accordingly, and do not compare a CHIRPS "global mean"
with one from a genuinely global dataset such as TerraClimate.
:::

| | |
|:--|:--|
| Version | v3.0 |
| Spatial resolution | 0.05 degrees, ~5 km |
| Grid | 2400 x 7200 = 17.3 million cells |
| Coverage | 60S-60N, all longitudes |
| Temporal resolution | Monthly (daily and pentad also published) |
| Record | 1981 to present |
| Latency | ~10-13 days after the month ends |
| Units | mm/month |
| Source | [data.chc.ucsb.edu/products/CHIRPS/v3.0](https://data.chc.ucsb.edu/products/CHIRPS/v3.0/) |

For SPI you need one variable, precipitation, so there is no PET step and no
water balance. That makes CHIRPS considerably less work than TerraClimate.

::: {.callout-tip}
## This is the low-latency option

CHIRPS publishes monthly, roughly a fortnight after the month ends. Measured
publication dates for the last four complete months, checked 2026-09-29:

| Month | Published | Days after month end |
|:--|:--|--:|
| May 2026 | 12 June 2026 | 11 |
| June 2026 | 14 July 2026 | 13 |
| July 2026 | 14 August 2026 | 13 |
| August 2026 | 11 September 2026 | 10 |

The `by_year` NetCDF is rewritten as each month lands, so `chirps-v3.0.2026.monthly.nc`
held 8 months when checked, at 131.3 MB against ~195 MB for a complete year.

For comparison, TerraClimate releases one file per calendar year and the current
year is absent entirely: on the same date its newest data was 2025. If you are
monitoring an ongoing drought rather than studying the record, that difference
decides it. See [Preparing TerraClimate](00b-terraclimate.qmd#terraclimate-or-chirps-for-spi).

There is no preliminary monthly CHIRPS at this path: a request for the
current month returns 404 until the final product is published.
:::

---

## Two distributions, same data

CHC publishes monthly CHIRPS in two forms. Both give the same numbers; they
differ in how much you download and how much preparation each needs.

| | NetCDF | GeoTIFF |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Layout | One file for everything, or one per year | One file per month |
| Size | 8.9 GB whole, or ~197 MB per year | 23.1 MB per month |
| Full record 1981-2025 | ~8.9 GB | ~12.5 GB (540 files) |
| Coordinates | `latitude` / `longitude` | n/a, needs building |
| Missing data | Declared via `_FillValue` | **Not declared.** Uses -9999 |
| Packed integers | No | No |
| Work to prepare | Rename coordinates | Stack, build a time axis, mask -9999 |

**Use the NetCDF unless you have a reason not to.** The GeoTIFF route exists
because some pipelines already work in tiles, or because you want a handful of
months rather than the whole record.

::: {.callout-note}
## The scripts on this page

Helpers live in `docs/tutorials/scripts/`. Imports below assume you are working
from `docs/tutorials/`; adjust the path or copy the modules next to your code.
:::

---

## Route A: NetCDF

### Download

::: {.panel-tabset}

#### By year

Preferred. Resumable, restartable, and you can start work before the whole
record has arrived.

```bash
for y in $(seq 1981 2025); do
  wget -c "https://data.chc.ucsb.edu/products/CHIRPS/v3.0/monthly/global/netcdf/by_year/chirps-v3.0.${y}.monthly.nc"
done
```

```bat
for /L %y in (1981, 1, 2025) do wget -c ^
  "https://data.chc.ucsb.edu/products/CHIRPS/v3.0/monthly/global/netcdf/by_year/chirps-v3.0.%y.monthly.nc"
```

#### Single file

One 8.9 GB download covering the whole record. Simple, but a dropped connection
at 80% costs you everything unless your client resumes.

```bash
wget -c "https://data.chc.ucsb.edu/products/CHIRPS/v3.0/monthly/global/netcdf/chirps-v3.0.monthly.nc"
```

#### Python

```python
from pathlib import Path
from scripts.tc_prepare import download_year   # generic, not TerraClimate-only

BASE = ("https://data.chc.ucsb.edu/products/CHIRPS/v3.0/monthly/"
        "global/netcdf/by_year")

out = Path("raw")
for year in range(1981, 2026):
    download_year("chirps-v3.0", year, out, base=BASE)
```

`download_year` builds `{base}/{var}_{year}.nc`, so for CHIRPS pass the stem and
rename, or call it as a template. For a one-off, `wget -c` is less fuss.

:::

### Prepare

CHIRPS NetCDF is already unpacked, already in mm/month, and already on a regular
monthly axis. Two things need attention.

**The coordinates are `latitude` and `longitude`**, not `lat` and `lon`. The
package auto-detects either, but standardising once keeps everything downstream
simple.

**Merging the yearly files** needs the time axis sorted and checked.

```python
from pathlib import Path
import xarray as xr
from scripts.nc_fixups import standardise_names, clean_missing, write_cf_metadata

files = sorted(Path("raw").glob("chirps-v3.0.*.monthly.nc"))
ds = xr.open_mfdataset(files, combine="by_coords", engine="netcdf4")

ds = standardise_names(ds)          # latitude -> lat, longitude -> lon, CF attrs
ds = clean_missing(ds, "precip")    # -9999 and friends -> NaN
ds = write_cf_metadata(
    ds,
    title="CHIRPS v3.0 monthly precipitation",
    institution="Climate Hazards Center, UC Santa Barbara",
    source="CHIRPS v3.0",
    references="Funk et al. (2015), Scientific Data 2, 150066",
)

ds["precip"] = ds["precip"].astype("float32")
ds.to_netcdf(
    "wld_cli_chirps3_precip_1981_2025.nc",
    encoding={"precip": {"dtype": "float32", "_FillValue": -9999.0,
                         "zlib": True, "complevel": 5,
                         "chunksizes": (ds.sizes["time"], 128, 128)}},
)
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Alternative: CDO

```bash
cdo -z zip_5 mergetime chirps-v3.0.*.monthly.nc wld_cli_chirps3_precip_1981_2025.nc
ncrename -d latitude,lat -d longitude,lon -v latitude,lat -v longitude,lon out.nc
```

Faster, and fine here because CHIRPS needs no unpacking. You give up control of
the output chunking, which matters if you will read per-pixel time series: see
[Preparing Your Data](00-data-preparation.qmd) on chunking for how you read.
:::

---

## Route B: GeoTIFF

One file per month, named `chirps-v3.0.{yyyy}.{mm}.tif` with a zero-padded
month.

### Download

```bash
for y in $(seq 1981 2025); do
  for m in 01 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 10 11 12; do
    wget -c "https://data.chc.ucsb.edu/products/CHIRPS/v3.0/monthly/global/tifs/chirps-v3.0.${y}.${m}.tif"
  done
done
```

```bat
for /L %y in (1981, 1, 2025) do for %m in (01 02 03 04 05 06 07 08 09 10 11 12) do ^
  wget -c "https://data.chc.ucsb.edu/products/CHIRPS/v3.0/monthly/global/tifs/chirps-v3.0.%y.%m.tif"
```

540 files, about 12.5 GB.

### The trap in this route

::: {.callout-warning}
## The GeoTIFFs use -9999 and do not declare it

Read straight from the remote file:

```
declared nodata : None
dtype           : float32

location                        lon     lat          value
mid Pacific ocean           -140.00    0.00     -9999.0000
south Atlantic ocean         -25.00  -40.00     -9999.0000
Amazon, land                 -60.00   -3.00       347.3873
Sahara, land                  10.00   23.00         0.3212
above the band (Arctic)       0.00    59.50     -9999.0000
```

Because no nodata tag is set, **every reader treats -9999 as a measurement**.
Nothing errors. You get an ocean of negative rainfall, a global mean that is
meaningless, and if it reaches a distribution fit, a result that is confidently
wrong.

So pass the sentinel explicitly:

```python
tiffs_to_netcdf(..., nodata=-9999.0)
```
:::

The second trap is the half-pixel shift, covered in
[Preparing Your Data](00-data-preparation.qmd#convert-to-netcdf-if-needed).
CHIRPS makes it concrete: the geotransform origin is exactly `-180.0, 60.0`,
which is the **corner** of the first pixel. Its **centre** is
`-179.975, 59.975`. Copy the origin into a coordinate array and every cell is
2.5 km out of position.

### Convert

```python
from scripts.tiff2nc import tiffs_to_netcdf

tiffs_to_netcdf(
    "tifs/",
    "wld_cli_chirps3_precip_1981_2025.nc",
    var_name="precip",
    glob="chirps-v3.0.*.tif",
    date_pattern=r"chirps-v3\.0\.(\d{4}\.\d{2})\.tif",
    date_format="%Y.%m",
    units="mm",
    standard_name="precipitation_amount",
    long_name="monthly precipitation",
    nodata=-9999.0,               # not declared in the file
    lat_order="descending",       # keep the GeoTIFF row order
)
```

The date pattern captures `1981.01` and `%Y.%m` parses it, so the files sort by
real date rather than by filename. `tiffs_to_netcdf` also verifies every raster
shares the first file's grid, which matters across a 540-file download where one
partial file would otherwise be stacked in silently.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Alternative: GDAL

```bash
gdalbuildvrt -separate chirps.vrt chirps-v3.0.*.tif
gdal_translate -of netCDF -a_nodata -9999 chirps.vrt chirps.nc
```

Quick, and it gets the cell centres right. What you do not get is a time
coordinate: the bands come out as `band1..band540` with no dates attached, so
you still have to build the time axis yourself before any index code will read
it.
:::

---

## Check before you compute

```python
import numpy as np
import xarray as xr

ds = xr.open_dataset("wld_cli_chirps3_precip_1981_2025.nc")
p = ds["precip"]

print(f"dims    : {p.dims} {p.shape}")
print(f"time    : {str(p.time.values[0])[:10]} to {str(p.time.values[-1])[:10]}")
print(f"units   : {p.attrs.get('units')}")
print(f"lat     : {float(p.lat.min()):.3f} .. {float(p.lat.max()):.3f}")

last = p.isel(time=-1).values
print(f"finite  : {np.isfinite(last).sum():,} of {last.size:,}")
print(f"range   : {np.nanmin(last):.2f} .. {np.nanmax(last):.2f} mm")

# The check that catches the GeoTIFF trap.
assert np.nanmin(last) >= 0, "negative rainfall: the -9999 sentinel got through"
# And the one that catches a truncated stack.
expected = (2025 - 1981 + 1) * 12
assert p.sizes["time"] == expected, f"{p.sizes['time']} steps, expected {expected}"
```

A correct CHIRPS v3.0 monthly series over 1981-2025 has **540 time steps** on a
**2400 x 7200** grid, with latitude spanning -59.975 to 59.975.

---

## What you should have

```
wld_cli_chirps3_precip_1981_2025.nc    precip, float32, (540, 2400, 7200)
```

Unpacked (CHIRPS never was packed), in mm/month, NaN over ocean and outside the
60S-60N band, coordinates named `lat` and `lon`, and 540 monthly steps.

That is the input contract for `spi()`. CHIRPS needs no PET and no water
balance, so there is nothing further to prepare.

::: {.callout-note}
## One CHIRPS-specific thing to carry forward

CHIRPS has many exact zeros, in arid regions and in the dry season everywhere.
Gamma is undefined at zero. This package handles that for you by fitting a mixed
distribution and carrying the zero probability separately, so **do not**
pre-substitute a small value such as 0.001 - see
[Preparing Your Data](00-data-preparation.qmd#replace-zeros-only-if-you-must).
:::

## Next step

Your data is ready. The calculation itself, including calibration periods,
multi-scale SPI, distribution choice and saving fitting parameters for
operational reuse, is [Calculate SPI](01-calculate-spi.qmd).

For the whole global grid rather than a region, the tiled and concurrent routes
are described in [Implementation](../technical/implementation.qmd#dask-run-phase-by-phase).

To clip to a country or basin first, see
[Preparing Your Data](00-data-preparation.qmd#by-shapefile). The boundary rule
matters more than it looks.
